content.p: The Black Pistons Motorcycle Club is an outlaw motorcycle club that works as a support club for the Outlaws Motorcycle Club. Police in Canada and the United States describe the Black Pistons as closely tied to the Outlaws, and the club's own account, police briefings and news reports give different pictures of its size and reach.

According to the club's own UK website, the first Black Pistons chapters were formed in Germany on 19 February 2002, with five chapters at the start. The same account says that a Columbus, Ohio group called Satan's Syndicate was the first in the USA to change its patches and join, and that a second chapter opened in Ocala, Florida, soon after. The first American clubhouse, the website says, opened in Shelbyville, Kentucky, on 19 August 2002.

The club's account says the UK chapters began in February 2003, when a side-patch club in Birmingham called The Brotherhood saw ten of its members patch over. It also says that many members later moved up to full Outlaws membership, and that by 2007 only three members remained in the Cotswolds. The club says it was rebuilt from 2009. These are the club's own statements; independent reporting does not confirm the membership figures.
content.h2: A support club for the Outlaws
content.p: The Outlaws Motorcycle Club was founded in 1935 in McCook, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago. WANE 15 reported in 2025 that the club had grown to more than 1,700 members in 176 chapters in the United States and abroad, a figure it attributed to the U.S. Justice Department. The Justice Department labels the Outlaws an outlaw motorcycle gang and lists the Black Pistons among the other such groups. WANE 15 reported that the Black Pistons back the Outlaws and help the parent club bring in new people.

Membership in the Outlaws follows a set path. A prospect first becomes a hangaround, then a probationary member, and only a unanimous vote of a chapter makes him a full member. WANE 15 described that path using court documents from earlier Outlaws cases.
content.h2: Chapters in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick
content.p: In July 2018, CBC News reported that a new Black Pistons club had recently opened in Cape Breton and was affiliated with the Outlaws. The report said that many friend and support clubs in Nova Scotia were tied to either the Bacchus or the Hells Angels, and that RCMP expected a Black Pistons club to open in the Halifax area. RCMP Const. Scott Morrison had made these points in a presentation to the Halifax Board of Police Commissioners.

CBC News reported later that month that the Outlaws operate in New Brunswick through the Black Pistons, which police said had a support club chapter in Fredericton. The same report said the Halifax presentation included a map of violence between the Angels and the Outlaws. According to the map, violence between Angels Quebec members and the Black Pistons erupted somewhere in the Fredericton area in October 2016. The map showed four violent incidents in the Fredericton area, one in the eastern part of the province and one in Nova Scotia. Morrison told the board that the New Brunswick chapter had been established longer than the Nova Scotia one, and that a lot of the activity had taken place there.

Fredericton police declined an interview and said the content had not been provided or approved by their force. New Brunswick RCMP said they had not been called to any violent clashes between outlaw motorcycle gangs, while acknowledging ongoing criminal investigations they could not discuss. CBC also reported arrests in the wider outlaw-gang investigation in New Brunswick. Police allege that Robin Moulton is a full-patch member of the Hells Angels Nomads chapter in New Brunswick, and that Emery Martin is a long-standing member of the Angels in Quebec. CBC reported that neither man had been convicted of the charges against him.

In November 2013, Niagara police carried out a raid that CHCH called a "massive bust." Niagara police called the operation Project Resurgence. It began with the St. Catharines Street Crime Unit, which had noticed drug trafficking and home invasions in the city since January that year that bore the mark of an Outlaws group. Police raided about 30 locations across Niagara, using more than 200 officers from forces across southern Ontario.

CHCH reported that police announced 150 charges and 31 arrests. Among those arrested was Randy McGean, whom CHCH described as the Black Pistons ring leader. McGean's wife was also arrested at their St. Catharines home. CHCH reported that nine of those charged were Black Pistons members and that the club's clubhouse at 80 Page Street was raided. Police said the seized items included cocaine, heroin, marijuana, cash, an AK-47 type assault rifle and a Mach 10 .45-calibre automatic weapon fitted with prohibited over-capacity magazines.

Police put the total value of the seized items at $18 million. Staff Sergeant Shawn Clarkson of the Niagara Regional Police told CHCH: "It is our belief that the Black Pistons organization would have been a full patch Outlaws chapter by the end of November." Police said the weapons were used for intimidation. Niagara Regional Police Chief Jeff McGuire said outlaw motorcycle gangs were not welcome in the region. CHCH reported that police believed the raids had squashed the Black Pistons' attempt, and the wider Outlaws' attempt, to gain a foothold in the region.
The reports of the arrests do not say how the cases against the people arrested ended. Anyone charged in those cases is presumed innocent unless and until a court decides otherwise.

The Black Pistons' ties to the Outlaws are best understood against the parent club's history in court. In August 1995 a federal jury in Florida found 14 members and associates of the Outlaws guilty on counts that ran from small marijuana sales and cocaine trafficking to illegal gun transfers and a plot to firebomb a rival club's headquarters. The same jury could not agree on the main charge, that the Outlaws were a racketeering conspiracy, and a mistrial was declared on more than 20 counts. Two defendants were acquitted of all charges.

A second federal trial in Florida opened in September 1997 against four members, including a former regional president, on racketeering charges. Federal prosecutors alleged that the Outlaws were an ongoing criminal enterprise whose activities included murder, extortion, drug trafficking and gun running. They were expected to use testimony from a former Florida Outlaws president, Wayne Edward Hicks, on the club's structure. Defence lawyers in the earlier 1995 trial portrayed the investigation as overreaching, and some jurors later complained that some defendants had been drawn into government-staged drug transports.

In 2011 a federal judge sentenced Jack Rosga, the national president of the Outlaws, to 20 years in prison. A jury had found him guilty in December 2010 of conspiring to engage in racketeering and conspiring to commit violence in aid of racketeering. The U.S. Attorney's Office in Virginia said 27 people had been charged in the investigation, and that twenty had pleaded guilty or been convicted at trial by the time of the sentencing. The office said the Outlaws had planned shows of force against rival clubs, particularly the Hells Angels.

The Black Pistons were founded in Germany, where authorities have banned several outlaw motorcycle clubs. A Maastricht University blog published in 2017 said that in Germany, a state interior minister can ban an association whose aims or activities conflict with criminal law, and that such a ban allows the authorities to seize the club's assets. The blog said that in 2012 and 2015 bans hit a Bandidos chapter, a Hells Angels chapter and several of their support clubs. In 2015, it said, authorities issued the first national ban on a whole motorcycle club, Satudarah, which came originally from the Netherlands.

The blog also argued that bans may not stop organized crime. It said members of banned clubs in some cases simply switch to another club, and that a support club can take over when the main club is removed. Authorities in Germany are not reported to have banned the Black Pistons or one of their chapters.

The club's own account and the police accounts differ on how many chapters it has and how large it is. The club lists chapters in many countries, while the police reports describe chapters tied to specific cities. Police in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia gave different statements about the same violence, and Fredericton police did not confirm the Halifax presentation. Public reports do not give the current membership, the current chapter list, or the outcome of the Niagara cases.
